studies.question: When going for it on 4th down gains win probability, how often do NFL teams go?
studies.answer: In states where going gains 1+ point of WP, teams went 25% of the time in 2015-16 and 45% in 2024-25.
findings: In clear-kick states, teams go about 4% of the time every season (n=15,129).
WP lost to clear errors was 4.6 points per team-game in 2015-16 (4.3-4.9) and 3.4 in 2024-25 (3.2-3.7).
In the 2023-26 go states, the go rate is 76% at 4th-and-1 (n=1,195), 39% at 2-3 yds (n=1,420) and 24% at 4+ (n=1,719).
studies.method: For each play, the expected WPA of going (pooled conversion rate x WPA if converted or failed) against the best of a punt or FG, each from boosted models of nflverse WPA on the same pre-snap state, cross-fit by game. A team's own choice doesn't set the rate. The CIs on WP lost exclude model error.
studies.data: nflverse play-by-play, 2015 to 2026 wk 8, Q1-Q4 4th downs (no penalties/kneels), 44,765 plays, 3,148 games.
studies.split_check: The model checks out of sample: on realized WPA in go states, teams that went are +1.3 points and teams that kicked are -1.3 (n=4,866/8,682). The rise in the go rate holds every season.

rq.a: In states where going gains 1+ point of WP, teams went 25% of the time in 2015-16 and 45% in 2024-25.
rq.note: n = 44,765 · go % by season (going gains 1+ WP pt)

studies.question: Down 14, a team scores a touchdown. Should it go for two right away or kick?
studies.answer: Go for 2. Given two TDs and a stop it wins 59% of the time against 46% for kicking, worth +3.2 points of win chance overall.
findings: The gain given two TDs is +13.3 points (+10.8 to +15.7), and going for 2 first wins as long as the 2-pt rate is above 35.2%.
After a Q4 PAT at down 8 the same team scored the next TD with nothing between in 24% (n=199); in the rest the choice decides almost nothing.
Inputs: 2-pt 48.1% (n=1,476), XP 94.4% (n=14,843), and teams that tied late won 47% in overtime (n=161).
Teams went for 2 at down 8 in the 4th in 0 of 35 in 2015-16 and 16 of 30 in 2025-26.
Raw results are noisy: teams that went for 2 won 5 of 48 and teams that kicked won 19 of 151, and the teams that chose each differ.
studies.method: A closed-form tree given two TDs and no opponent score: after 2 is good, kick to win; after 2 fails, 2 again to tie; after an XP, kick to tie; overtime at 50%. The CI comes from Beta draws of the 2-pt and XP rates. The game-level edge is the share of down-8 spots that reach a second TD first, times the gain.
studies.data: nflverse play-by-play, 2015 to 2026; 1,476 2-pt tries, 14,843 XPs, 199 Q4 PATs at down 8.
studies.split_check: The gain is +13.1 points with the 2015-20 rates (2-pt 47.6%) and +13.5 with the 2021-26 rates (2-pt 48.6%); with the measured overtime rate it is +15.1.

studies.answer: AUC is .92+ at QB, WR, TE, DL, LB and DB, 0.82 on the offensive line and 0.75 at running back.
findings: Pro Bowl AUC is lower everywhere: OL WAR 0.73, DB 0.80, QB 0.86.
studies.method: The AUC of the season value against AP first-team All-Pro, among players with 400+ snaps at the position group, with seasons pooled. The 90% interval comes from resampling seasons. XV uses no AV. WAR is .6 AV WAR + .4 XV, and AV carries an All-Pro bonus.
studies.data: Site NFL board replayed 2018-25 (nflverse); AP All-Pro teams and Pro Bowl rosters from Wikipedia; 6,665 player-seasons.
studies.split_check: The intervals are across seasons. OL and RB sit below every other group in both WAR and XV.

studies.question: Do surprise onside kicks get recovered more than expected late-game onside kicks?
studies.answer: Yes, 25% against 9% (2015-23), but that is below the ~32% break-even for an early onside. Net WPA isn't different from zero.
findings: Surprise onsides were recovered 25.0% of the time (15.5-37.7, n=56), and expected ones 8.9% (6.7-11.6, n=508).
On a Q1-Q3 surprise onside, the kicking team's WPA is -0.6 points (-1.8 to +0.6, n=54). A normal kickoff is -0.04.
The break-even recovery rate for a Q1-Q3 surprise onside is about 32%.
In 2024-26, 6.3% of expected onsides were recovered (3.2-11.9, n=127).
studies.method: An onside is a kickoff described as onside. Expected means Q4 with the kicking team trailing, and surprise is all the others. WPA is compared with normal Q1-Q3 kickoffs within 14 points, with game bootstrap CIs. Teams pick their spots, so the rates are upper bounds.
studies.data: nflverse play-by-play, 2015 to 2026 wk 8, 691 onside kicks.
studies.split_check: Surprise recovery was 28% in 2015-18 (n=32) and 21% in 2019-23 (n=24). Expected stays near 9%.

studies.question: On 3rd or 4th and 1, does the QB sneak convert more often than other plays?
studies.answer: Yes. Sneaks convert 82% of the time, other runs 69% and passes 56%. The sneak share of these plays went from 8% in 2015 to 14% in 2025.
findings: Passes convert 56.3% (54.4-58.2, n=2,612). The gap between sneaks and other runs is +12.5 points (+10.1 to +14.9).
EPA per play: sneak +0.33 (+0.23 to +0.42), other run +0.04, pass -0.14.
Without PHI and BUF, sneaks still convert 81.1% (78.7-83.3, n=1,102).
studies.method: A conversion is a first down or a TD, on the same down and distance. Reweighting to the sneak's mix of down and goal-line state gives 82/69/57%. A yards to go of 1 hides inches, so sneaks may get the shortest spots.
studies.data: nflverse play-by-play, 2015 to 2026 wk 8, 3rd/4th-and-1 runs and passes, WP 5-95%, 10,488 plays.

rq.q: On 3rd or 4th and 1, does the QB sneak convert more often than other plays?
rq.a: Yes. Sneaks convert 82% of the time, other runs 69% and passes 56%. The sneak share of these plays went from 8% in 2015 to 14% in 2025.
rq.note: n = 10,488 · converted % by season (QB sneak)

studies.question: Is a two-point try worth more than an extra point on average?
studies.answer: There is no clear edge. A 2-pt try scores 0.96 points per try and an XP scores 0.94, a difference of +0.02 (-0.03 to +0.07).
findings: 2-pt success is 48.1% (45.5-50.6, n=1,458), and the break-even against the XP is 47.2%.
The 2-pt rate by season ranges from 41% to 55%, and every season's CI includes 48%.
2-pt runs convert 55% (50-60, n=388), and passes 45% (42-48, n=1,041).
studies.method: Wilson 95% CIs on the success rates. Expected points are 2 x the 2-pt rate against the XP rate. Tries are from Q1-Q4 in all game states. Selection is small, since 2-pt tries are mostly driven by the score.
studies.data: nflverse play-by-play, 2015 to 2026 wk 8, 1,458 two-point tries and 14,618 extra points.

rq.q: Is a two-point try worth more than an extra point on average?
rq.a: There is no clear edge. A 2-pt try scores 0.96 points per try and an XP scores 0.94, a difference of +0.02 (-0.03 to +0.07).
rq.note: n = 16,076 · points per try by season (two-point try)

studies.question: Does a recruiting class's top end win more than its depth?
studies.answer: No. Point for point they are worth the same: CFB t = 0.70, CBB t = 0.51. The plain sum is not beaten.
findings: CFB, four classes on a roster: top 5 0.044 rating SD per 10 points, depth 0.027 (n=1,605).
CFB class sum over no class score: t = 3.49, 13/13 seasons. No reweighting passes (best t = -0.20).
CBB, returning and transfer value held fixed: top 2 0.071, depth 0.049 per 10 points (n=1,546).
CBB without the roster held fixed, depth reads -0.084: a deep class follows a thin returning roster.
studies.method: Program rating z (opponent-adjusted margin in CFB, net rating in CBB) on the class's top-end and depth FV points, with the ratings before signing, a three-season baseline and program level as controls. Forms that reweight the class (split, decay, cap, star premium, power x decay) were pre-registered and scored held out by class or season, t clustered by program.
studies.data: CFBD composite classes 2009-25 and cfbfastR results 2005-25; consensus-ranked CBB classes 2009-25 and program net ratings 2008-26. 1,605 CFB program-seasons, 1,546 CBB classes.
studies.split_check: CFB NIL-era seasons: top 5 0.069, depth 0.006, t = 1.49 (n=511). Not distinguishable yet.

studies.question: Down 14, a team scores a touchdown. Should it go for two right away or kick?
studies.answer: Go for 2. Given two TDs and a stop it wins 56% of the time against 48% for kicking, worth +1.7 points of win chance overall.
findings: The gain given two TDs is +8.0 points (+6.2 to +9.8), and going for 2 first wins as long as the 2-pt rate is above 36.8%.
After a Q4 PAT at down 8 the same team scored the next TD with nothing between in 20% (n=484); in the rest the choice decides almost nothing.
Inputs: 2-pt 44.3% (n=3,017), XP 97.5% (n=47,908), and teams that tied late won 52% in overtime (n=245).
Teams went for 2 at down 8 in the 4th in 1 of 94 in 2016-17 and 2 of 34 in 2026.
Raw results are noisy: teams that went for 2 won 9 of 52 and teams that kicked won 43 of 432, and the teams that chose each differ.
studies.method: A closed-form tree given two TDs and no opponent score: after 2 is good, kick to win; after 2 fails, 2 again to tie; after an XP, kick to tie; overtime at 50%. The CI comes from Beta draws of the 2-pt and XP rates. The game-level edge is the share of down-8 spots that reach a second TD first, times the gain.
studies.data: cfbfastR play-by-play, FBS against FBS, 2016 to 2026; 3,017 2-pt tries, 47,908 XPs, 484 Q4 PATs at down 8.
studies.split_check: The gain is +8.3 points with the 2016-20 rates (2-pt 44.3%) and +7.8 with the 2021-26 rates (2-pt 44.3%); with the measured overtime rate it is +6.7.

studies.question: Up 3 in the last 12 seconds, should the leader foul or defend?
studies.answer: There is no clear edge. The leader wins 92.7% of the time fouling and 91.4% defending, +2.3 points at equal time (CI -2.4 to +6.4).
findings: Leader win rate: 92.7% fouling (CI 88.5%-95.5%, n=219) and 91.4% defending (CI 89.9%-92.6%, n=1585).
The difference at the same time left (foul minus defend) is +2.3 points (95% CI -2.4 to +6.4).
The game reached OT 9.6% of the time after a foul and 14.3% after defending. The leader lost in regulation 1.8% and 1.6% of the time.
Once in OT, the leader won 42.9% after fouling (n=21) and 50.4% after defending (n=226).
studies.method: The sample is the first trailing-team possession of each game that is live with 12 seconds or less left in the final regulation period, down 3. A foul is the leader's non-shooting foul that sends the trailing team to the line before any shot. Fouling and defending are compared within possession-start bins (4-8, 8-12, 12+ s), and the outcome is the game win, including OT.
studies.data: ESPN play-by-play via sportsdataverse, NBA, 2011-12 to 2025-26, 1,804 games.
studies.split_check: Foul minus defend was -0.4 points in 2012-19 (CI -10.0 to +7.4) and +2.8 in 2020-26 (CI -2.9 to +7.7).

studies.question: Does a timeout stop an opponent run?
studies.answer: No. After a run of 8+ points, a timeout nets -0.31 points over the next 2:00 compared to playing on (CI -0.40 to -0.23).
findings: With a timeout, the next 2:00 nets +0.51 points (CI +0.44 to +0.58), n=9313.
With no timeout, the next 2:00 nets +0.83 points (CI +0.79 to +0.87), n=23790.
Both groups outscore the opponent after the run (mean reversion, plus they have the ball). The gap at the same state is -0.31.
In Q4 only, timeout minus none is -0.26 points (CI -0.42 to -0.10), n=6980.
studies.method: The trigger is a score that makes an unanswered run of 8+ points, with at least 2:30 left in the quarter and the margin within 20. A timeout in that dead ball is compared to no timeout in the next 60 s, on net points over the next 120 s, matched on run size and quarter.
studies.data: ESPN play-by-play via sportsdataverse, NBA 2011-12 to 2025-26, 16,242 games, 33,103 runs.
studies.split_check: Timeout minus none was -0.32 points in 2012-19 (CI -0.44 to -0.22) and -0.31 in 2020-26 (CI -0.42 to -0.19).

studies.question: How do the in-season award odds (NBA, NFL, NHL, CFB) compare with traded prices?
studies.answer: The market is far ahead. Winner log loss was 2.34 for the model and 1.22 for Polymarket on the 2025-26 races.
findings: Held 2025-26: 19 race-checkpoints over 10 races. The model was 2.345 and the market 1.218, and the market was better in 7 of 10 (t = 2.44).
Tuning 2024-25: 17 race-checkpoints over 7 races. The model was 2.045 and the market 1.098.
A temperature fit to the market (T 1.5) didn't help on outcomes. The held change was -.07 (t = -.53).
The first CFB backtest (2005-25, 246 checkpoints) had the favourite at .33/.37/.42, against a hit rate of .11/.24/.31, at 25/50/75%.
studies.method: The races are rebuilt as of 25/50/75% of each season, with voter fits that leave one season out (scripts/awards_asof.py). The market is the Polymarket (global) daily price of the eventual winner on the day after the checkpoint, renormalised over the listed candidates. Checkpoints whose prices sum more than 25% off 1 are dropped as illiquid.
studies.data: scripts/data/poly_hist (36 closed events, 2024-26); nflverse, in-repo NBA boxes, sportsdataverse ESPN CFB boxes.
studies.split_check: The market was ahead in both seasons (2024-25 and 2025-26).

studies.question: With 25-40 seconds left in a quarter, does a quick shot for a 2-for-1 pay?
studies.answer: Yes. A quick shot nets +0.33 points per quarter-end compared to a full possession (CI +0.26 to +0.39).
findings: A quick shot (<=10 s) nets +0.61 points to the end of the quarter (CI +0.56 to +0.66), n=6896.
A full possession (>10 s) nets +0.35 points (CI +0.32 to +0.38), n=13048.
Points for and against: 1.85/1.24 quick, 1.25/0.90 full.
On all start types, transition included, quick minus full is +0.34 points (CI +0.31 to +0.37), n=53737.
studies.method: The sample is the first possession starting with 25-40 s left in Q1-Q3. The outcome is own points minus opponent points to the end of the quarter. The main sample is inbounds after an opponent score (no transition), with quick and full possessions compared within 5 s start-time bins and a game-clustered bootstrap.
studies.data: ESPN play-by-play via sportsdataverse, NBA 2011-12 to 2025-26, 19,166 games, 19,944 inbound possessions.
studies.split_check: Quick minus full was +0.32 points in 2012-19 (CI +0.24 to +0.41) and +0.34 in 2020-26 (CI +0.24 to +0.43).

studies.question: Up 3 in the last 12 seconds, should the leader foul or defend?
studies.answer: Foul. The leader wins 93.6% of the time fouling and 92.4% defending, +2.8 points at equal time (CI +0.8 to +4.6).
findings: Leader win rate: 93.6% fouling (CI 92.0%-94.9%, n=1063) and 92.4% defending (CI 91.7%-93.1%, n=6053).
The difference at the same time left (foul minus defend) is +2.8 points (95% CI +0.8 to +4.6).
The game reached OT 6.7% of the time after a foul and 14.2% after defending. The leader lost in regulation 3.1% and 0.9% of the time.
Once in OT, the leader won 50.7% after fouling (n=71) and 52.7% after defending (n=857).
studies.method: The sample is the first trailing-team possession of each game that is live with 12 seconds or less left in the final regulation period, down 3. A foul is the leader's non-shooting foul that sends the trailing team to the line before any shot. Fouling and defending are compared within possession-start bins (4-8, 8-12, 12+ s), and the outcome is the game win, including OT.
studies.data: ESPN play-by-play via sportsdataverse, CBB, 2011-12 to 2025-26, 7,116 games.
studies.split_check: Foul minus defend was +2.2 points in 2012-19 (CI -0.6 to +4.8) and +3.3 in 2020-26 (CI +0.7 to +5.8).

studies.question: Does a timeout before a late free throw make the shooter miss?
studies.answer: Icing doesn't work. Iced shooters were +2.3 points better than un-iced shooters, relative to their own FT% (CI +0.0 to +4.6).
findings: Iced shooters made 71.2% (CI 68.9-73.4), against their usual 72.5%, n=1567.
Shooters who weren't iced made 69.9% (CI 69.5-70.2), against their usual 73.4%, n=59853.
Iced minus not iced, against their own FT%, is +2.3 points (95% CI +0.0 to +4.6).
studies.method: The sample is the first FT of a trip in the last 2:00 of regulation or OT, with the margin within 3. A shooter is iced when the defense calls timeout between the foul and the FT. The outcome is made minus the shooter's leave-one-out FT% (min 20 other FTs), with a game-clustered bootstrap.
studies.data: ESPN play-by-play via sportsdataverse, CBB, 2011-12 to 2025-26, 61,420 first free throws.
studies.split_check: Iced minus not iced was +2.0 points in 2012-19 (CI -1.0 to +4.8) and +2.5 in 2020-26 (CI -0.8 to +6.1).

studies.question: When should a trailing team pull its goalie?
studies.answer: Pull at 3:18 down one and at 6:27 down two. Teams pull at 1:52 and 2:39.
findings: Down 1 at 5v5 in the last 10 min: 2.35 GF/60 (2.14-2.58) and 1.98 GA/60, over 12,201 min.
The CI on the optimum is 2:42-3:57 down 1 and 4:42-9:04 down 2. Only 2% of down-1 pulls (n=1,801) come that early.
The gain over actual timing from 10:00 left, down 1, is +0.6 points of tie chance (0.2 to 1.2).
studies.method: The outcome is being level or ahead at 60:00. A per-second Markov model on goal rates by state (6v5, 5v5 down 1/2, tied), with game-cluster bootstrap CIs. The model matches what was observed: down 1 at 6:00, it predicts 22.5% against an observed 24.4% (n=1,523).
studies.data: NHL API play-by-play + shift charts, regular seasons 2021-22 to 2024-25, 5,248 games; pull times from goalie shifts.
studies.split_check: The optimum down 1 was 3:10 in 2021-23 and 3:26 in 2023-25. The median actual pull went from 1:47 (2021-22) to 1:58 (2024-25).

rq.q: When should a trailing team pull its goalie?
rq.a: Pull at 3:18 down one and at 6:27 down two. Teams pull at 1:52 and 2:39.
rq.note: n = 5,248 · level at 60:00 % by minutes left when pulled (down 1)

studies.question: Should a team down one late pull its goalie on a power play?
studies.answer: Yes, with 3:00 or less left. 6v4 adds 8 points of tie chance at 2:00. Past 4:00 the gain isn't clear.
findings: 5v4 trailing in the 3rd period: 8.5 GF/60 (7.9-9.1) and 1.2 GA/60, over 5,159 min.
On a minor with 2:00 left, down 1, a team is level at 60:00 31% of the time at 6v4 and 24% at 5v4 (difference CI 3 to 12 points).
On a minor with 4:00 left, the gain is +3.7 points (-0.4 to 7.6), which I can't tell apart from zero.
studies.method: The outcome is being level or ahead at 60:00. A Markov model of a 2:00 minor, 6v4 against 5v4 followed by the optimal even-strength pull, with rates from trailing teams in the 3rd period. 6v4 time is chosen late, so its rates carry selection.
studies.data: NHL API play-by-play + shift charts, regular seasons 2021-22 to 2024-25, 5,248 games.
studies.split_check: The gain at 2:00 left was +9 points in 2021-23 and +6 points in 2023-25.

studies.question: After the 2023 base and pickoff rules, do runners still steal too little?
studies.answer: Slightly. Steals of 2nd succeed 75.9% of the time against a 71.7% break-even, worth +2.6 runs per team-season. With 1 out there is no edge.
findings: Attempts per PA with a runner on 1st only went from 6.0% to 8.3%. Success fell each year: 77.2%, 75.8%, 74.8%.

studies.method: Steal attempts from clean states (runner on 1st only, or 2nd only), including pickoff-CS and K+CS. The break-even comes from era RE24 (innings 1-8). Run value uses the steal outcome only. Average success above the break-even doesn't prove the marginal try pays.

studies.question: Do intentional walks gain win probability for the defense?
studies.answer: Mostly no. With a runner on 2nd and 1 out, the IBB costs the defense 2.0 points of win probability. In the other states there is no gain I can tell apart from 0.
findings: Runner on 2nd, 1 out: -2.0 points (CI -3.3 to -0.7), n=545 IBB. Late and close it is -4.1 points (CI -7.1 to -1.2).
2nd and 3rd, 1 out: +1.3 points (CI +0.9 to +1.8) over the PA, but +0.3 (CI -0.8 to +1.4) to the end of the inning.
IBB batters are +15 points of season wOBA over the other batters in these states, which is in the model.
IBB per season: 826 in 2016 and 393 in 2025 (non-pitcher batters, innings 1-9).
studies.method: The change in empirical WE from the defense's view, from the start of the PA to the end of the half-inning (main) and over the PA. An OLS with batter and on-deck season wOBA and inning x score x season cells, with SE clustered by game. The comparison is pitching to the batter in the same state.
studies.data: Retrosheet play-by-play, 2015-2025 regular season, 6,129 intentional walks to non-pitchers in innings 1-9. Retrosheet: the information used here was obtained free of charge from and is copyrighted by Retrosheet (www.retrosheet.org).
studies.split_check: Runner on 2nd, 1 out: -2.0 points in 2015-19 and -1.9 in 2020-25 (SE 0.8, 1.2).

studies.question: Does the times-through-the-order penalty justify pulling starters before the 3rd time?
studies.answer: For an average starter, yes. The 3rd time through is +.022 wOBA over the 1st for the same pitcher, .339 against .323 for relievers.
findings: Within a pitcher-season, the 2nd time is +.013 wOBA over the 1st (CI +.011 to +.016) and the 3rd time is +.022 (CI +.020 to +.025).
Pitch count adds nothing: -.004 (CI -.012 to +.004) per 100 pitches, and the 3rd time stays at +.025.
The jump at batter 19 was +.017 (SE .003) in 2015-19 and +.000 (SE .003) in 2020-25, when it became a smooth rise.
Batter-adjusted wOBA: starters .321 the 1st time and .339 the 3rd time, relievers in inning 6+ .323 (n=664,061).
studies.method: An OLS on PA wOBA with pitcher-season fixed effects, batter-season wOBA, platoon and home, with SE clustered by game. The starters who survive to the 3rd time are having better days, so if anything the penalty is understated.
studies.data: Retrosheet play-by-play, 2015-2025 regular season, 1,109,963 starter PAs (1st-3rd time), 24,958 games. Retrosheet: the information used here was obtained free of charge from and is copyrighted by Retrosheet (www.retrosheet.org).
studies.split_check: The 3rd-time penalty was +.024 in 2015-19 and +.020 in 2020-25. The discrete jumps are only in 2015-19.

studies.question: Do sacrifice-bunt tries with nobody out gain win probability?
studies.answer: No. A bunt try costs 0.3 to 0.9 points of win probability compared to swinging, and up to 1.9 late and close.
findings: Runner on 1st, 0 out: -0.3 points (CI -0.4 to -0.1), n=5,068 tries of 107,555 PAs.
Runner on 2nd: -0.7 points (CI -1.0 to -0.4). 1st and 2nd: -0.9 points (CI -1.1 to -0.6).
1st and 2nd, 7th inning on, within 1 run: -1.9 points (CI -2.8 to -1.0), n=700 tries.
On realized WE to the end of the inning, no CI excludes 0 (1st: -0.2 points). The try rate was 9.1% in 2015 and 6.5% in 2025.
studies.method: Non-pitcher PAs with 0 out in innings 1-9. A bunt try is a bunt in play or a foul or missed bunt. The outcome is the change in empirical WE over the PA. An OLS with batter and on-deck season wOBA and inning x score x season cells, with SE clustered by game.
studies.data: Retrosheet play-by-play, 2015-2025 regular season, 158,989 PAs with runners on and 0 out, 9,669 bunt tries. Retrosheet: the information used here was obtained free of charge from and is copyrighted by Retrosheet (www.retrosheet.org).
studies.split_check: There is a PA-level loss in both eras for 2nd and for 1st+2nd. Runner on 1st: -0.5 points in 2015-19 and -0.0 in 2020-25 (n.s.).

studies.question: Does a team leading by one goal lose the xG battle late, and does it cost points?
studies.answer: Yes, after 75'. Its xG share is 46% against an expected 53%. That costs 0.05 xPts from 75', but the actual points held.
findings: Leading by 1, 75-90+: xG share 45.9% (CI 43.2%-48.4%) against an expected 52.7%, over 1434 matches.
Leader xG/90 in 75-90+: 1.16 for and 1.38 against. In 15-45' the share is 57% and 55%, against an expected 54%.
Up 1 at 75' (n=1041): xPts is 2.55 from realized xG against 2.60 at strength rates, a gap of -0.05 (CI -0.08 to -0.03).
Actual points were 2.60 (CI 2.55-2.65) against a 2.60 baseline (gap 0.00). The late xG lost doesn't show up in the results.
studies.method: 11v11 minutes only, split by score state and 15-min band. The expected share comes from both teams' leave-one-out season xG for and against, a home factor and league xG volume by band. xPts is a Poisson on the remaining xG, with CIs bootstrapped by match.
studies.data: StatsBomb open data, 23 full seasons/tournaments (2015/16 EPL, Serie A, Ligue 1; men's WC/Euro/Copa/AFCON; ISL; women's leagues and tournaments), 2,856 matches with clean event data.
studies.split_check: The xPts gap from 75' was -0.08 in the 2015/16 men's leagues (n=401) and -0.04 in the other competitions (n=640). Both CIs exclude 0.

studies.question: Do deep completions add to xG and market ratings in the soccer game model?
studies.answer: No. Every weight raised 1X2 log loss on 2015-22 (+.02 to +.46 x1000), so it was never taken to the held-out seasons.
findings: The best setting (gain .08, weight .03) was +.02 x1000, t by day .39, better in 4/8 seasons, over 19,466 matches.
At a weight of .10 it was +.19 to +.46 x1000 (t up to 2.29). More weight on deep completions is worse.
Moving .05 of the xG weight to deep was +.21 x1000, t = 1.61. Deep is weaker than xG at the same weight.
In the base model the market ratings carry ~.89 of the blend and xG .11, so a process stat has little room.
studies.method: Deep completions (Understat 'deep', passes completed within ~20 m of goal) are put on the goal scale by one ratio (.234 goals per deep, big five 2015-22) and walked as a fifth side rating like xG. They are scored on 90-minute 1X2 log loss, paired by match, with t from match-day sums. The grid was pre-registered, and held 2023-26 is untouched.
studies.data: ESPN results + football-data closes + Understat team match histories, big five 2015-22 scored with UEFA matches; 21,359 matches with deep counts.
studies.split_check: No setting beat the base in more than 4 of 8 seasons.

studies.question: Do teams score more or less in the minutes after a goal?
studies.answer: There is no momentum swing. The team that just conceded scores at 0.95x its baseline in the next 10 min, and the scorer at 1.06x. The restart dips the first 3 min.
findings: The team that conceded, 0-10 min: xG 0.92x baseline (CI 0.88-0.96), goals 0.95x (CI 0.88-1.02).
The team that scored, 0-10 min: xG 0.99x (CI 0.95-1.03), goals 1.06x (CI 0.99-1.12).
In the first 3 min after a goal both teams sit below baseline (xG 0.74x and 0.87x), which is the restart.
There is no sign that a team is most vulnerable just after it scores. Its opponent's goals in 0-10 min are 0.95x baseline.
studies.method: Team-minutes (11v11) by time since the last goal. The baseline is the league rate for the same 15-min band and score state, scaled by pre-match strength (leave-one-out season xG). Results are observed over expected, with CIs bootstrapped by match.
studies.data: StatsBomb open data, 23 full seasons/tournaments (2015/16 EPL, Serie A, Ligue 1; men's WC/Euro/Copa/AFCON; ISL; women's leagues and tournaments), 2,856 matches, 527,256 team-minutes.
studies.split_check: The conceding team's goals in 0-10 min were 1.09x in the 2015/16 leagues and 0.88x elsewhere. The direction flips, so there is no stable effect.

studies.question: When do teams make their first sub by score state, and does an early first sub pay off?
studies.answer: Trailing teams make their first sub by 60', and level and leading teams by 65'. A first sub before 60' adds +0.04 of xG difference, and I found no effect on goals.
findings: First tactical sub at HT: trailing 34.4% (n=1606), level 16.0% (n=2206), leading 13.0% (n=1582).
Subbed by 60' if the state held: trailing 60%, level 36%, leading 30%.
A sub before 60' against none, from 60' to the end: xG diff +0.041 (CI +0.005 to +0.078), goal diff +0.045 (CI -0.02 to +0.11), n=4,853.
Trailing at 60': +0.070 xG diff (CI +0.004 to +0.136, n=1699). HT subs against none: +0.052 (CI -0.002 to +0.105).
studies.method: Timing is a discrete hazard of the first tactical sub per minute by the current state. The effect is a landmark at 60' (and HT): an OLS with match-clustered SE on score state, strength, home, prior xG diff, the xG diff in the 15 min before the landmark (the trigger window) and an early opponent sub. Injury subs and red cards before the landmark are excluded.
studies.data: StatsBomb open data, 23 full seasons/tournaments (2015/16 EPL, Serie A, Ligue 1; men's WC/Euro/Copa/AFCON; ISL; women's leagues and tournaments), 2,659 matches, 4,853 team-matches at the 60' landmark.
studies.split_check: The xG-diff effect was +0.028 in the 2015/16 leagues and +0.048 elsewhere. The sign is the same, and neither CI excludes 0 alone.

rq.q: When do teams make their first sub by score state, and does an early first sub pay off?
rq.a: Trailing teams make their first sub by 60', and level and leading teams by 65'. A first sub before 60' adds +0.04 of xG difference, and I found no effect on goals.
rq.note: n = 4,853 · teams subbed by minute (trailing)

studies.question: Should players hit a first serve on second serve?
studies.answer: No. 1 of 188 men and 0 of 112 women gain with a CI above 0. The median player loses 6.8 points per 100 (men) and 5.3 (women).
findings: Men: 152 of 188 lose with a 95% CI below zero, and 1 gains with a CI above zero.
Women: 80 of 112 lose with a 95% CI below zero, and 0 gain with a CI above zero.
Pooled men: a 1st serve wins 44.6% per attempt, against 51.0% for a 2nd.
Pooled women: a 1st serve wins 40.0% per attempt, against 45.4% for a 2nd.
studies.method: For each server: P(1st in) x P(win | 1st in) minus P(2nd in) x P(win | 2nd in), with a bootstrap 95% CI resampling matches. It assumes the first-serve in-rate and win rate hold on second-serve points.
studies.data: Match Charting Project points, 1960-2026 (71% of matches 2015+), 11,785 matches; servers with 500+ second serves.
studies.split_check: Gainers by era (250+ 2nd serves), pre-2015 / 2015+: men 4 of 104 / 14 of 193, women 3 of 42 / 7 of 169.

studies.question: Do players drop serve more often right after breaking?
studies.answer: No. For the same player and match, the hold rate after breaking is +0.7 points (men) and +0.5 (women) higher than after the opponent holds.
findings: Men: +0.7 points (95% CI +0.2 to +1.2), 11,796 player-matches.
Women: +0.5 points (95% CI -0.2 to +1.2), 7,616 player-matches.
The raw hold rate after breaking is 82.0% for men and 69.1% for women, which is mostly stronger servers doing the breaking.
studies.method: Holds (non-tiebreak games) by whether the server broke in the previous game. It is a weighted difference within each player-match, with a bootstrap CI resampling matches. Form swings within a match bias this upward.

rq.a: No. For the same player and match, the hold rate after breaking is +0.7 points (men) and +0.5 (women) higher than after the opponent holds.

studies.question: Do first serves wide, body and T win at equal rates, as mixed-strategy theory predicts?
studies.answer: Wide and T do, within 1 point for the same server. Body doesn't. It is 4.2 points lower for men and 4.1 for women.
findings: T minus wide within a player: men -0.1 points (SE 0.1, 498 player-sides), women -0.4 (SE 0.2, 311).
Wide and T differ at p<.05 for 8% of men's and 7% of women's player-sides, where 5% is expected by chance.
Body minus wide/T for the same server: men -4.2 points (SE 0.2), women -4.1 (SE 0.2).
Body is 10% of men's and 20% of women's first serves, and charters may log missed targets as body.
studies.method: The outcome is the server winning the point, given the first serve was aimed at that target (faults count). The within-player test compares wide and T for each server and court side (150+ serves each).
studies.data: Match Charting Project points, 11,785 charted matches, 1,857,004 first serves with a direction.
studies.split_check: Wide and T are within 0.4 points in both eras (pre-2015, 2015+), for men and women.

studies.question: How much is the first pistol round worth, and does the side matter?
studies.answer: The winner of the first pistol takes the map 59.5% of the time, 57.1% from the CT side and 61.9% from the T side.
findings: Pistol 1 won on CT: map win 57.1% (56.1%-58.2%, n=8,809).
Pistol 1 won on T: map win 61.9% (60.9%-63.0%, n=8,716).
A team that wins both pistols wins the map 69.3% of the time (n=8,912). When the pistols are split, the P1 winner wins 49.4%.
Above the Elo expectation, P1 on T is +11.3 points and on CT +6.0. Winning P1 against losing it, Elo-adjusted, is +17.2 points (+16.0 to +18.6).
studies.method: Map win % for the pistol round winners (rounds 1 and 13), with Wilson CIs. Team strength is a logistic model on pre-map Elo, and the pistol effects are average marginal changes with map-clustered CIs.
studies.data: bo3.gg round data, S/A/B-tier pro maps, 2023-10-16 to 2026-11-02, 17,525 maps
studies.split_check: P1 winner map win: 59.3% early (n=8,762) and 59.7% late (n=8,763).

studies.question: After losing the pistol round, should the team save or buy on round 2?
studies.answer: Buying on round 2 is worth +26.8 points in round 2 and -16.5 points in round 3. The map win is -0.8 points, which isn't different from 0.
findings: CT buy against save, adjusted: R2 +25.0 points (+24.0 to +25.9), R3 -17.0 points (-18.6 to -15.5). 66% of CT losers buy.
T buy against save, adjusted: R2 +28.3 points (+27.3 to +29.4), R3 -16.0 points (-17.6 to -14.5). 50% of T losers buy.
Map win, buy against save: CT -1.1 points (-2.6 to +0.3), T -0.8 points (-2.2 to +0.7).
First-half rounds won (of 12), buy against save: CT +0.30 (+0.20 to +0.40), T +0.27 (+0.17 to +0.37).
studies.method: The pistol loser's round-2 buy class comes from bo3.gg equipment value (a save is an eco, and a buy is a half or force buy). Logistic models adjust for side, team Elo, the winner's round-2 equipment, the loser's pistol kills and the half, with cluster-robust CIs by map.
studies.data: bo3.gg round data, S/A/B-tier pro maps, 2023-10-16 to 2026-11-02, 17,525 maps, 34,640 pistol-loss halves (16,992 CT)
studies.split_check: Map effect early / late: CT -1.1 points / -1.1 points, T +0.9 points / -2.6 points.

studies.question: What does a stand-in cost an ESEA team?
studies.answer: About 2 points beyond the five's own ratings, which is too small to help on held-out matches. Rate the five who play.
findings: After the five's player Elo and FACEIT level, the first stand-in is -0.09 log-odds (SE 0.04) and the second is +0.16.
Held S58-S59 log loss: t = -1.5, and leave-one-day-out t = -0.3. It didn't ship.
A stand-in's FACEIT level counts like a core player's, .59 against .54 log-odds per level (SE .08/.04).
studies.method: The core is the 5 most-used players in the team's prior 20 maps that season (no lookahead). A logistic on the five's round-share player Elo and FACEIT level plus the stand-in count, with walk-forward ratings.
studies.data: FACEIT ESEA NA league, S53-S59, 18,217 matches; 6,078 with both cores defined
studies.split_check: The first stand-in is negative in 4 of 5 seasons. A whole-season core (lookahead) inflates the raw gap to 54.9% against 50.1%.

studies.question: Does retuning the CS2 ARK rating every month beat keeping its settings fixed?
studies.answer: The monthly retune passes, and retunes ship monthly: -0.0018 log loss per series, t by month -8.66 (bar -2.00), through 2026-10.
findings: It won 16 of 16 months. On top-50 series, t = -0.06.
The calibration slope is 0.964 on 15,957 scored series.
Settings picked: span 0.3 (14 months), K 384 (2 months).
Shipped: span 0.3.
studies.method: Each month, the settings with the lowest log loss on all earlier series are picked from the shipped set and from one-step moves on K, K decay, map K, lower-tier K, region K, span and new-player start. They are then scored once on that month against the shipped settings.
studies.data: Valve VRS series + bo3.gg maps, Aug 2024 to 2026-10, 15,957 walk-forward series.
studies.split_check: 16/16 months better, top-50 t = -0.06.

studies.question: How much does an equipment gap change round win chances on CT and T?
studies.answer: Full buy against full buy, the CT side wins 51.7%. At equal dollar value the CT side wins 48.5%, and an eco beats a full buy 5.6% of the time.
findings: Full buy against full buy: the CT side wins 51.7% (51.4%-52.0%, n=154,499).
Force against full: a CT force wins 36.0% (35.4%-36.5%, n=28,386), and a T force wins 36.0% (n=40,093).
Eco against full: a CT eco wins 5.9% (5.5%-6.4%, n=11,243), and a T eco wins 5.4% (n=17,966).
The CT side needs about $1.3k more equipment value than the T side for a 50% round, since CT rifles and kits cost more.
studies.method: Non-pistol regulation rounds. Each team's equipment value at the start of the round comes from bo3.gg, binned by CT minus T in $4k steps (ends capped at $24k). Round win rate with map-clustered CIs.
studies.data: bo3.gg round data, S/A/B-tier pro maps, 2023-10-16 to 2026-11-02, 17,525 maps, 327,073 rounds
studies.split_check: CT win % in full against full: 51.7% early (n=76,815) and 51.7% late (n=77,684).

studies.question: Does a losing streak hurt the next round beyond economy (the no-timeout baseline)?
studies.answer: There is no tilt. After 3+ straight losses a team wins +0.9 points more than an economy and score model expects.
findings: After 1 loss in a row, teams win 35.8% against a model 36.3%, a gap of -0.4 points (-0.7 to -0.2, n=136,681).
After 3 losses in a row, teams win 39.5% against a model 38.5%, a gap of +1.1 points (+0.7 to +1.5, n=51,700).
After 5 losses in a row, teams win 40.8% against a model 40.0%, a gap of +0.8 points (+0.1 to +1.6, n=15,367).
The bo3.gg round data has no timeout calls, so the timeout effect itself isn't measured.
studies.method: A logistic baseline on the buy-class matchup by side, equipment values, score gap, Elo and round in the half. The result is the actual minus the predicted win rate by the current losing streak in the half, with map-clustered CIs.
studies.data: bo3.gg round data, S/A/B-tier pro maps, 2023-10-16 to 2026-11-02, 17,525 maps, 327,073 rounds
studies.split_check: The 3+ streak gap was +0.9 points early (n=55,017) and +0.9 points late (n=55,026).

studies.question: Which side should a team start on, map by map?
studies.answer: Start on T. Teams that start on T win 52.4% of maps, from 55.8% on overpass down to 50.0% on anubis.
findings: All maps: the T-first team wins 52.4% (51.6%-53.1%, n=17,525).
The CI excludes 50% on inferno, nuke, dust2 and overpass. Elo-adjusted, T-first is +2.5 points.
studies.method: Map win % of the team that started on T, with Wilson CIs. The side choice isn't random (pick/veto), so Elo-expected wins are subtracted as a check on team strength.
studies.data: bo3.gg round data, S/A/B-tier pro maps, 2023-10-16 to 2026-11-02, 17,525 maps

studies.question: Does re-picking a rating's settings each season beat keeping them fixed?
studies.answer: It passes in CS2, NHL, CBB, and fails in Tennis, Soccer, NFL, NBA.
findings: CS2: -1.56 log loss ×1000, t by month -3.49, 13/16 months.
NHL: -0.65 log loss ×1000, t by month -2.85, 18/27 months.
CBB: -0.65 log loss ×1000, t by month -2.52, 27/36 months.
Tennis: -0.09 log loss ×1000, t by month -1.19, 26/46 months.
studies.method: Each season (each month in CS2), the settings with the lowest walk-forward log loss on every earlier season are picked from the shipped set and from one-step moves on each tuned setting. They are then scored once on that season against the shipped settings. Only held-out seasons count, and a sport passes at t by month <= -2.
studies.data: Each sport's game-model history, on held-out seasons before the 2026-27 lockbox. CS2 runs from Jul 2025 to its last sealed month.
studies.split_check: 3 of 7 sports pass.

rq.q: Does re-picking a rating's settings each season beat keeping them fixed?
rq.a: It passes in CS2, NHL, CBB, and fails in Tennis, Soccer, NFL, NBA.
rq.note: n = 95,174 · t by month by sport

entries.short: FV is a grade on the 20-80 scale of what a prospect becomes at his peak, set as the mean outcome of past players with the same profile.
body: 50 is an average regular, 60 is a plus player, 70 is a star and 80 is generational. Tiers are every 5 points and grades move in steps of 1.
Each board has its own outcome and rarity ladder. There is no shared FV scale across sports.
The headline is the mean of the tier odds, busts and stars included, so it sits below the best case.
The grade is absolute talent, read from a fixed map fit on pooled history, not a rank within a class or a board.
A strong class gets more high grades. Age and the drivers that pass held out move the grade.
entries.where: Every prospect board: CFB, CBB, hockey prospects, soccer prospects, tennis prospects; recruit tabs; MLB boards

charts.note: CBB held out: grade given vs outcome reached

entries.short: OVR is a 0-99 grade of a pro player's overall skill, read from his sport's most predictive rate. It is the pro counterpart of FV.
body: Replacement level is 60, the median starter is 75 and the best player in a typical season is 97. Between those points the grade is linear in the rate. Above 97 the upper slope carries on to a cap of 99, and below replacement the lower slope carries on to a floor of 20. The points are set on past seasons (NBA 2016-2026, NHL 2014-2026, soccer 2015-2022) so the scale holds still through a season.

The NBA reads pXPM, the NHL pWAR a 60 put on a full season at a starter's TOI for his position (F 1129, D 1440, G 3134 minutes), the NFL pXP/60, soccer p/90 put on a full season, tennis ARK as log-odds by tour, and CS2 the RWA rating. Putting the NHL and soccer on full seasons first keeps a defenseman and a forward on one scale of wins. Goalies have their own range (replacement 60, the median starting goalie 75, the best goalie in a typical season 97), because on the shared scale every starter sat at 86 to 89. The order is the same either way, and it is a weak one: held out, the goalie grade ranks next season's goalie WAR a 60 at a Spearman r of .17 (17 seasons, 1,500 minutes both years), against .48 for forwards and .43 for defensemen.

Each idea was tested leaving one season out and scored three ways: next season's rate, next season's value (rate times playing time), and team results. It was kept only when it was better on one of the three with t of 2 or more and worse on none past 1. In the NBA nothing beat pXPM alone: this season's XPM t = 1.15, age t = -1.55, position t = -0.06, and a slope that grows with career minutes lost on team results (t = -2.74). NHL forwards and defensemen take that slope (forwards: value r t = 23.48, team R² t = 4.93), goalies take age (t = -2.71), and this season's WAR added nothing to the fixed pWAR (forwards t = 1.41). Soccer takes this season's SV, age and position: next-season error t = -4.65, team R² 0.801 to 0.808 (t = 5.08), 6 of 7 seasons.

Starting rookies from their final draft FV, with its weight fading as pro minutes come in, failed in every sport against a plain rookie offset that fades the same way: NBA t = 0.66 on next season's rate, NHL forwards t = 0.54, soccer t = 3.33. Draft FV explains little of an NBA rookie's first season (r = 0.14 with his XPM). It is in the retests ledger.

The band is the 80% range on true talent. With the season's noise added it covers 81% (NBA), 81% (NHL forwards) and 81% (soccer) of next-season rates held out. The NBA O and D grades are the grade with the other side at the median starter's. Next season's offense is read better from this season's offense than from the total (error t = -21.1, 17 of 17 seasons), and defense the same way (t = -31.0).

The NFL, tennis and CS2 use their tested ratings as they are. The history on hand does not hold enough seasons to rerun these tests for them, so their points come from the current board: replacement is the snap-weighted mean of non-regulars for the NFL, #100 on ARK for tennis and the replacement line for CS2, and the starter is the median regular, #25 on ARK and the median tier-1 player. They are in the retests ledger.

Team OVR is the roster's player rates weighted by playing time, put on the same 0-99 points: a replacement roster 60, the median team 75 and the best team in a typical season 97. Four weightings were tested leaving one season out on next season's team result (NBA 2011 to 2025, NHL 2010 to 2025): minutes, last season's minutes, depth slots fit by position and equal weights on the top of the roster. Minutes won in both leagues, R² 0.699 in the NBA against 0.579 for last season's minutes (t = -5.17), 0.585 for depth slots and 0.584 for equal weights, and 0.522 in the NHL against 0.451 (t = -2.95), 0.364 and 0.383. The board weights by the minutes played so far this season. The NFL weights by snaps and CS2 takes the five players with the most maps.

OVR as an input to the team models did not pass. Weighted by minutes, it predicted next season's team result no better than the projection rate it is read from: NBA R² 0.699 against 0.699 (t = 0.25; in the NBA OVR is a straight line in pXPM, so it holds nothing new) and NHL 0.522 against 0.517 (t = 0.92, 6 of 13 seasons).

OVR is not an FV anchor yet. For 493 NBA rookies from the 2011 to 2024 drafts, the FV on file ranks OVR after three seasons at a Spearman r of 0.23, and the pre-draft rank does better on the same players (0.42, t = -3.94, FV ahead in 2 of 14 classes). FV 45 to 49 rookies were starters (OVR 75 or more) 54% of the time, and FV 30 to 34 rookies 16%.

A second round tried five more inputs against the live grade. Minutes a game (what his coaches think of him) passed in the NBA on team results (t = 4.72) and for NHL forwards on next season's rate (t = -4.34) and value (t = 4.85). Age times the rate passed in the NBA (t = -2.41), because a veteran's good rate carries forward less than a young player's. Last season's trend, a separate weight on defense and HPM beside pWAR did not pass, and nothing passed for defensemen, goalies or soccer.

NFL OVR is on one scale for every position. A slope for each position group on next season's team margin did not beat one slope for all of them (t = -0.25, 5 of 9 seasons). The running back slope came out at -1.68 (standard error 1.14) against 2.09 for all groups together, which says the board may give backs credit that belongs to the line, but a running back slope of its own did not pass either (t = -1.33, 6 of 9 seasons).
entries.where: NBA, NFL, NHL projections > OVR; soccer leaders > OVR; tennis ATP / WTA OVR; Counter-Strike RWA leaders > OVR

entries.short: The outcome ladder is the realized result each FV tier stands for, set by how rare it is on each board.
body: CFB: the NFL career (All-Pro, Pro Bowl, seasons as a starter), from the 2012-18 drafts.
CBB: peak NBA XPM, as rare as the matching NBA role (7+ All-NBA teams = 80), for careers ending 2008-16.
Hockey: peak NHL pWAR (best 3 of the first 7 seasons), by rarity in a draft class, 2008-19 classes.
Soccer: peak GAR at ages 22-26, by rarity in a birth year and position group, for players who were 22 in 2013-21.
Tennis: peak ranking points above No. 200 at ages 22-28, by rarity in a birth year on each tour, births 1979-97.
The ATP fit also trains on births after 1997, with partial careers imputed to a final outcome.
entries.where: fv model tab on each prospect page; FV conversion charts below

entries.short: Above each board's knot K the headline runs in a straight line to 80 at T, so an 80 comes about once every 5 seasons.
body: The mean of a capped outcome can never reach 80. The stretch makes 80 reachable, but rare.
K is the mean that about 3 players a season reach, and T is the level one player reaches about every 5 seasons (exponential tail, held out).
The order of players doesn't change. The exact mean (fvx) stays in the tooltips, and above K the headline reads higher than the realized means.
entries.where: Headline FV on every prospect board (data/fv_scale.json)

entries.short: Each player's odds of reaching every outcome tier, and his 10th to 90th percentile outcome.
body: CFB and CBB use a location-scale ordered probit of the realized outcome on the grade, with cut points at 30, 35 ... 70.
A spread term is kept only if it improves held-out RPS (CFB: early season ×2.1, walk-on, consensus, underclassman).
Held out, CFB RPS is .0398 compared to .0408 with one spread, and CBB is .0767. Hockey, soccer and tennis use logistic odds for each tier.
The odds are shown in the player dropdown only. The main boards show the single headline.

entries.term: Tier chances (NBA%, NHL%, Top%, Reg%, Star%)
entries.short: The chance a player reaches a set outcome tier.
body: CBB NBA% is the chance he plays in the NBA, the first rung of the FV model.
Hockey NHL% is the chance of 40+ (top 45 of a class), and Reg% is 50+ (an NHL regular, top 20 of a class).
Soccer Top% is 40+ (a top-flight regular, top 250 of a birth year at the position), Reg% is 50+ (top 90) and Star% is 60+ (top 20).
entries.where: Board columns: CBB, hockey prospects, soccer prospects

entries.short: A + marks a player whose odds of becoming a star beat those of a player 2.5 FV higher, because of his age.
body: The rule: + when P(60+ | FV, age) >= P(60+ | FV + 2.5). Age is the only upside signal that passed held out.
Held out, soccer is t = 5.0 / 4.1 at 55+ / 60+, tennis ATP t = 4.3 / 3.3 and WTA 3.9 / 3.1. About 6% of tennis prospects and 30% of the soccer top 2000 get one.
The CFB version failed held out (t = -.71 / -.34) and was removed. No signal passed in CBB or hockey.
entries.where: Soccer prospects and tennis prospects boards

entries.short: A player with only a birth year gets the mean birth day for his class, instead of Oct 15.
body: k = first D-I season - birth year - (class - 1).
Mean day of the year by k, from 16,744 day-precise careers: k 19 Apr 30, k 20 Jul 24, k 21+ Aug 22.
Held out on 942 board players who entered in 2023 or later,
mean absolute age error goes from .347 yr (Oct 15) and .258 (Jul 1) to .237 (t = 15.6 and 5.8).
FIBA youth rosters on file add a day-precise date when the birth year agrees with Barttorvik's.
1,401 of 1,427 checked dates were within 3 days.

entries.short: A player who isn't on the source board gets a provisional grade, which starts at the 20 floor and takes every driver available for him.
body: He is ranked in FV order with a prov tag. CBB uses a ridge on height, weight, class, age, recruit rank and the team's top-8 FV (R² .77).
Hockey grades OHL, WHL, QMJHL, AHL and Liiga draft-eligibles from Tankathon on NHLe, age, weight and position.
Soccer gives academy-only and youth-international players their own provisional line.
CFB grades ESPN roster backups and carried-over players up from the 20 floor.

entries.short: The CFB model grades every FBS and FCS player on his NFL outcome.
body: The composite is production (Stat+, Marcel 5/4/3, regressed), On3 talent, age, frame, combine, badges and the XV parts.
A player's composite rank in his class maps to FV through measured NFL outcome counts at each position (drafts 2012-18).
The scouting consensus (9 boards and the Kiper top 25) is blended in at a weight of .5 at full coverage.
Then comes the outcome step (ordered probit), the mean headline and the stretched top. Positional value scales elite RB, LB, DL, TE and S.
entries.where: CFB board, draft board, fv model tab

entries.short: The CBB model grades every D-I player and listed international on his NBA outcome.
body: E[FV] = 20 + 10 P(30+) + 10 P(40+) + 10 P(50+) + (mean 60+ career - 50) P(60+), with one ridge logistic for each rung.
Newcomers are graded on recruit rank (On3, 247, Barttorvik) and class. Returners add 3-season BPM, conference power, age, size and rates.
The board stage adds the June draft-board rank and guard combine testing. E maps to a grade on the pooled 2009-16 boards.
The outcome odds are fit on each board's top 300. Below that they scale down to the floor those boards realized (1.8% NBA).
In season, E = (1 - w) × preseason + w × now, with w = minutes / (minutes + k). k is 85 for newcomers and 156 for returners.
entries.where: CBB board, fv model tab, in season window

entries.short: An OLS on outcome FV for the draft class and for drafted players short of 100 NHL games.
body: The draft model keeps log slot (board rank as slot), defense, goalie, draft-year NHLe, class strength.
Leave-one-class-out error is 87.25, compared to 90.52 for draft slot alone (2008-19 classes, 2,541 picks).
After the draft, stage models add the latest NHLe, pro games, a World Juniors spot, NHL games and WAR so far.
entries.where: Hockey prospects board, drafted prospects, fv model tab

entries.short: An OLS on outcome FV for every under-22 in 33 leagues, plus academy and feeder leagues.
body: The inputs kept include age, market value (deflated to the level of the fit seasons), GAR this season and last,
minutes share, club strength, scoring rate, height, position and PL2 minutes. 53,682 rows, 2013-20.
The detailed position block (centre-back, full-back, defensive and attacking midfield, winger and striker, against central
midfield) cuts season-out error by -0.10 (t = 3.9, 7 of 8 seasons), and the top 50 and forward tests are better too.
The raw grade is the mean of the OLS grade and a gradient-boosted grade (300 trees of depth 3 on every design input,
one set for each snapshot). Season-out error goes from 55.62 to 54.62 (t = 8.7, 8 of 8 seasons). The trees get no missing-height
signal, and they see market values only as dated on a player's own lineups.
Held out by birth cohort, the error is 54.84, compared to 64.42 for age and market value alone (R² .43).
entries.where: Soccer prospects board, fv model tab

entries.short: A hurdle model for every ATP and WTA player under 22 with a ranking or a pro match in the last year.
body: A logistic for any peak value, then an OLS on outcome FV given value: FV = (1 - p) × 20 + p × mean given value.
ATP keeps age, rank, unranked, Elo, 52-week win rate, years since the pro debut and Futures volume.
WTA keeps age, rank, unranked, Elo, rank × age and tour-qualifying volume. Held out by birth year, OOS R² is .50 / .46.
Height is never an input, since the archive fills in height for the players who made it, which leaks the outcome.
The ATP fit also trains on unfinished careers (later births at imputed targets): as-of 2011-18 error goes from 21.45 to 20.24, t = 7.8, 8 of 8.

An ATP tree blend (the mean with a boosted-tree grade) went from 20.24 to 19.86 as of, t = 2.7, 7 of 8, p .015. It was a second form after the first failed, so it counts in the sweep's Holm family of 15 and misses the cut (p <= .005). It isn't used. The WTA trees failed going forward.
entries.where: Tennis prospects ATP and WTA boards, fv model tab

entries.short: Projected RWA over the next year against tier-1 starters, on the 20-80 scale (50 = an average tier-1 starter).
body: A prospect is a player under 20 with maps at S-tier events. The projection uses rating, age and the share of last year's rounds at S/A-tier events.
The S/A share is negative on top of the rating's tier lift (held t = -4.9). Rise and every stat line failed.
Cutoffs are quarterly, fit on 2024-25 and held out from Jul 2025. A term ships only if it clears the Bonferroni cut for its batch.
Badges (top 25% on a stat) were tested on prospects and on the main board. None passed, so CS2 shows none.

entries.short: The baseball boards are graded by hand on the FanGraphs 20-80 tiers.
body: There is no model. 80 is top 5 overall (7+ WAR a season), 60 is an All-Star (3.4-4.9) and 50 is an average regular (1.6-2.4).
Boards: 2026 draft hitters v1, U19 MiLB prospects and the White Sox org top 64, each in its article. Current prospect grades are on eephus.io.
entries.where: Baseball Articles (draft hitters, U19 MiLB and White Sox org articles); eephus.io

entries.short: Projected FV for high school recruits.
body: CFB xFV = P(on board) × FV if on + (1 - P(on)) × 20, in year 1, from a hurdle fit on the ESPN 2023-26 classes.
The CFB recruit profile is weighted on the NFL outcomes of the 2011-19 classes, and the board sets the level.
CBB uses a hurdle on consensus rank and old-for-class: P(reach NBA), then log(FV - 20) given NBA, trained on 2009-16.
entries.where: Recruits tabs: 2027-2029 classes, class rankings, recruit model

entries.short: A recruit star rating cut on what past recruits with the same profile became, instead of the industry stars.
body: CFB is cut on the recruit index (expected NFL outcome, 2011-19 classes). A class holds about 34 five-stars, 102 four-stars and 265 three-stars.
Share drafted in CFB, held out: 5-star+ 79%, 5-star 55%, 4-star 29%, 3-star 18%, 2-star 9%, 1-star 3%.
CBB is cut on FV. 5 = 2+ NBA seasons as a starter, 4 = reached the NBA, 3 = a D-I starter at BPM +3, 2 = played D-I, 1 = did not.
There are half stars inside each tier. The arrow is ARK stars minus industry stars.

Past classes are graded back to 2008, so a college player carries his high school grade (HS). A CFB class has 3,039 to 4,031 graded recruits, from ESPN's class lists, the 247 composite and On3's team commit lists.
A recruit off ESPN's signee list with no ESPN grade gets a correction to his draft odds. Fit on 2011-19, tested forward on 2020-21 (2,101 recruits): t = 4.94 by recruit, 3.09 clustered by school.
Share drafted in the 2020-21 classes against expected: 1-star 2.0% (2.3%), 1.5-star 4.8% (5.5%), 2-star 8.1% (8.5%), 2.5-star 15.0% (12.2%).
Reading a lone service's grade on the industry scale failed (t = -1.92 clustered by school), so it is not used.
A player no source lists is a 1-star. Kickers, punters and long snappers get no grade.
CBB past classes read the rank to stars curve at the recruit's industry rank. No rank is a 1-star.
entries.where: Recruits tabs; recruit cards; HS column on the portal tabs

entries.short: The tier above five stars, for recruits at even odds or better of the top pro outcome.
body: CFB: a five-star with a 50%+ chance of a top-64 pick. There are about 6 a class. Held out, 57% went top 64 and 79% were drafted (plain five-stars 29% and 55%).
The chance reads the recruit index, the log industry rank and the industry rating past 95. Held out by class 2011-21: school-clustered t = 2.22, 9/11 classes. The 2022 class has 4 of 4 top-64.
Top-64 rate for the top 3 of a class: 79% with the industry terms, 58% on the index alone and 70% on industry rank. Top 6: 55%, 52%, 55%.
CBB: FV 41.43+, about 5 a class. Held out, 62% became NBA starters (2+ seasons) and 42% reached FV 55+ (plain five-stars 26%).

The CBB line was re-tested on the same even-odds rule. A line at FV 43.5 (3.2 a class) hits 69%, but the recruits between the two lines hit 50% and the six-tier R² falls from 0.318 to 0.297, so the line stays.
Position at the top failed in both: CFB quarterback and line flags t = -0.63, CBB big and point guard flags t = -0.92.

entries.short: A recruit's age on Sep 1 of the class year, minus the class median. Positive means old for the class.
body: The median is 18.84 in CBB (1,723 ranked recruits 2009-16) and 18.67 in CFB (1,415 top-400 recruits who reached the NFL).
CBB NBA rate at about the same rank: 38% under 17.9, 31% at 18.2-18.6 and 18% at 19.0+.
The CBB model input is old for the class (18+ on Oct 26 of the senior year), held out t = 2.65, 6/8 classes.
Continuous age in its place is t = 1.19, added on top t = 1.20, and a young flag t = 0.84 (gate 2.0). None of them shipped.
CFB top-64 pick rate given an NFL entry: 28% at 18.0-18.4 and 20% at 19.2+. Draft slot t = 1.75, 6/9.
CFB doesn't use it. It is short of the gate, and On3 lists an age for 34 of the top 300 in the latest class read.
Birth dates come from On3's whole-year age, bounded tighter by each daily reading, plus FIBA youth rosters and pins.
Cards show age against the class once the birth date is known to within 45 days. Hockey late birthdays and soccer birth month failed.

entries.short: A class's commits' FV points over the floor, summed. Top end and depth are its two parts.
body: CFB sums xFV - 20 and CBB sums expected FV points. Top end is the best 5 commits in CFB and the best 2 in CBB, and depth is the rest.

Both parts were tested against results: program rating z, with the ratings before signing, a three-season baseline and program level as controls, held out and clustered by program. Reweightings were pre-registered: split, decay by rank in class, cap, star premium (points to a power), average + size, power x decay.

CFB, the four classes on a roster (2013-25, n = 1,605): the sum beats no class score at t = 3.49, 13 of 13 seasons. A top-end point is worth 0.0044 rating SD (SE 0.0015) and a depth point 0.0027 (SE 0.0011), difference t = 0.70.
Per standard deviation that is 0.17 rating SD for top end and 0.11 for depth. Raw correlation with the season's rating: 0.54 and 0.43; after the controls 0.24 and 0.23.

No CFB reweighting beats the sum: split t = -1.59, decay t = -0.52, cap t = -1.82, star premium t = -0.20, power x decay t = -2.15. One class at a time (2012-22, n = 1,357) the best is t = 0.03. Quarterback and line points next to the sum: t = -3.09.

CBB, one class at a time (2012-23, n = 1,342): discounting depth looks better (power x decay t = 2.52, 9 of 12 classes) and a depth point reads -0.0084. That is roster turnover: a deep freshman class follows a thin returning roster.

With returning and transfer value held fixed (first season, n = 1,546), a CBB top-end point is worth 0.0071 (SE 0.0022) and a depth point 0.0049 (SE 0.0028), difference t = 0.51, and every discount loses: decay t = -1.03, cap t = -2.47, star premium t = 0.19, power x decay t = -1.32.
CBB rating bends with the class total (diminishing returns, t = 4.40), which changes no class's order. CFB does not bend (t = 0.31).

The sum stays the class score in both sports, and top end and depth stay descriptive ranks. Lead: in NIL-era CFB seasons a top-end point is worth 0.0069 and a depth point 0.0006 (t = 1.49, n = 511); retest after the 2027 season.
Second pass, same test. Another value basis does not beat the one in use: CFB FV if on the board t = 0.09 and year-3 xFV t = -1.06; CBB headline FV t = 1.28 and Y1 FV t = -0.48. Blends fail too.
Program development times the sum: CFB t = -1.91, CBB t = 0.77. Early and late commits weighted apart: t = -1.20 and -0.40. CBB enrol rate of the three classes before: t = 0.79.

Incoming transfers next to the class, first season: CBB passes at t = 6.45, 12 of 13 classes (NIL era t = 4.76). A unit of transfer value is worth 7.8 class points, and per standard deviation transfers move the rating 0.17 SD to the class's 0.08. CFB incoming transfer production: t = 0.73.

That is a net class (high school commits plus transfers), not a change to the high school score. Not testable on stored history: positional need against the returning roster, decommit risk, per-recruit Transfer% and Ret%.
History points are the live model's by composite rating and level (CFB) or consensus rank (CBB); against the live class scores r = 0.966 and 0.997.
entries.where: Recruits tabs: class rankings; class rankings GFX

entries.short: Bronze to platinum trait medals next to the name, each on one stat, regressed by volume.
body: The tiers are the 75th, 90th, 97th and 99th percentile of the position. CFB badges build archetypes.
On the other boards a badge shows only if it predicts the sport's own outcome held out, beyond the value metric.
They are display only, and no badge feeds FV or a projection. Volume and usage traits pass, and efficiency rates mostly fail.
entries.where: Every board (medals by the name), player cards

entries.short: Each player's grade at his best season, listed by position.
body: CFB rebuilds every FBS season 2014-25, with the box-score era (2014-18) means recalibrated to NFL outcomes.
The CFB outcome is NFL AV a season since the draft over a class horizon index h (mean 1 on the 2020-23 drafts), so years an old class spent out of the league don't count against it.
The other boards read their past lists, and only grade-complete rows are used.
entries.where: all-time FV tab on CFB, CBB, hockey, soccer and tennis prospect pages

entries.short: A draft class ranked on its draft-day grades, as the FV points over 40 that grades like them became.
body: Each class is the all-time FV list at its draft, each player once at his draft-day grade. A grade counts for the mean of (Out - 40)+ among past players graded the same, so in the latest era a 70 is worth 29 (CFB), 22 (CBB), and 28 (hockey) and a 50 is worth 14, 9, and 12.

Top is the class's 10 best grades, depth is grades 11 to 50, and overall is the two together. Fifty is about how many players on the lists go in the first two NBA or NHL rounds, and a fixed fifty keeps the size of each year's pool (thinner in the CFB box-score years) out of the ranks.

The points are fit by grading era, because a noisier grade of 45 is worth more than a sharper one: more of those players land well above 40. CFB splits the box-score lines (drafts 2015-19) from PFN's (2020 on), CBB splits the classes graded with their own class held out (2009-16) from the ones graded forward, and hockey is one era. A class with an outcome is fit without its own class.

Calibration is the log of career points over draft-day points, over every listed player of a class. On one pooled fit it falls 3.4% a year (t = -1.80) in CFB and 4.0% a year (t = -2.58) in CBB; fit by era it falls 1.3% (t = -0.58) and 1.9% (t = -1.07). Hockey has one era and falls 2.2% a year (t = -1.84); its newer classes have had fewer seasons to reach a peak.

The era check is the spread of overall ranks across the earliest, middle and latest third of the classes (Kruskal-Wallis H), against the 95% line of 10,000 era-blind shuffles: CFB H = 1.08 on a line of 5.65 (pooled fit 5.12), CBB H = 2.99 on a line of 5.72 (pooled fit 5.51), and hockey H = 3.50 on a line of 5.65 (pooled fit 3.50). All three pass, and so does what the classes became.

Became is the same sum on the careers, the class's 10 and 50 best outcomes whoever was graded where, once the class has one. Draft-day overall against became, classes with an outcome: r = 0.77 (CFB, 9 classes), -0.59 (CBB, 12 classes), and -0.07 (hockey, 12 classes). Classes under eight seasons from their draft are marked provisional. On the complete classes alone r = 0.80 (CFB, 4), -0.57 (CBB, 10), and -0.06 (hockey, 11), and with the draft year held fixed r = 0.71, -0.50, and 0.12. Year held fixed means the partial r of draft-day and became over every class with an outcome.
Strongest on draft day: CFB 2017, CBB 2015, and hockey 2016. Strongest careers among the complete classes: CFB 2017, CBB 2009, and hockey 2015. CFB covers QB, RB, WR, TE, EDGE, DT, and LB.
entries.where: all-time FV > draft classes on CFB, CBB and hockey prospect pages

entries.short: Wins over a replacement starter in a 12-game season.
body: WAR = snap share × (line + weight × quality) × .227. One point of margin a game is worth .0189 win% (928 FBS team seasons).
The line is the margin a team loses when an average starter sits: QB 2.7, RB 1.7, EDGE 1.4, WR 1.35, CB 1.3, S 1.1, DT 1.0, LB 1.0.
Quality comes from Stat+, badges and FV. The QB keeps 1.25 points per SD, and the rest goes to his offensive teammates by snaps.
A replacement lineup wins .18 (2 of 12), and an average team's starters add up to 3.8 WAR.
In team WAR, starter time that no graded player covers counts one SD below an average starter (season AV's line), instead of at
the WAR line. Held out by season 2019 to 2025, team WAR tracks SRS at R² .654, compared to .639 (t = 3.5, 7 of 7 seasons).
entries.where: CFB board, WAR leaders tab, team talent

entries.short: WAR minus snap share × line, which is wins over an average starter at the position.
body: It compares across positions, and a below-average starter is below 0.

entries.short: WAR with quality taken from the parts of the stat line that track winning.
body: CFB: the PFN score plus position parts (QB cmp %, yds/att and INT rate, OL pressure rate, DT splash, CB yds/target).
It is fit on 2024-25 team margin. Held out, team r is .88 compared to .86 for WAR quality, and win% r is .73 compared to .68.
NFL: the same idea, fit to team margin a game. On missed games it is t = 4.9, compared to 2.1 for AV WAR.
Next-season forecasts tie with WAR, so the projections and the game models stay on WAR.
The NFL weights are fit for each side: offense parts on points scored a game, and defense parts on points allowed a game.
XV from weeks 1 to 9 on the margin from week 10 on goes from R² .604 to .622 (t = 2.19, 7 of 8 seasons), and next-season team R² from .235 to .258.
Held out, XV is the most descriptive NFL metric (.604, compared to .401 for WAR and .257 for SV) and the most descriptive CFB one (.689, compared to .639 for cWAR).
entries.where: CFB and NFL WAR leaders tabs (XV column)

body: AV WAR = (AV - replacement AV at the sub-position × snap share) × .091 wins per AV.
The .091 comes from team wins on team AV (160 team seasons 2021-25, r .86). A replacement team wins 3 of 17.

entries.short: xNIL is what a player is worth on the NIL market now, yNIL is his estimated pay entering the season, and zNIL = xNIL - yNIL.
body: xNIL = position price × on-field value (AV at FV, × playing time), shared within the P4 and G5 pools.
yNIL splits each program's budget by a preseason index. The budget is the school's reported one: 68 P4 football programs (mean $27.2M) and 80 high-major basketball programs (mean $13.7M).

Without a report it is assumed: $3M in the G5, $0.4M in the FCS, $2.3M for a mid-major and $0.25M for a low-major in basketball. The mid-major level is The Athletic's coach survey, and it puts the 90th and 75th percentile player outside the power conferences within 1% of the College Sports Commission's report. The survey's low-major level put the median player at three times the reported one, so it was not used.

Football position prices are moved, against the other positions, to what schools report paying: RB -42%, WR -23%, TE -27%, DL -34%, EDGE -34%. On3 prices those positions higher. The defensive line is scored with linebackers, since schools list edge players as either.

The budget pays the whole roster. A provisionally graded football backup is paid 5% of the median graded player at his position on the team, and a kicker or punter 20% of the team's median graded player, rising 10% per FV point. Both shares were set on the College Sports Commission's pay percentiles. Their xNIL shares the group's own pay by worth, so a backup's or a specialist's zNIL is against his group's going rate.

A reported deal (13 on file, read from headlines every three hours and held back unless a national outlet or two outlets carry it) moves the player half way from the model's number to the report: his yNIL when the deal is for this season, his xNIL when it was reported in the last year. It also enters the price fit, so a position's price follows the reports between On3's repricings. On3 moved toward each of the three reports it trailed.
A budget list from an earlier season is carried forward at the market's growth (11% a year).
It isn't fit to On3 valuations, since those only move +18% per 10 FV. zNIL growth is 20% of each coach score.
Checked against the College Sports Commission's pay percentiles by position, On3 valuations and reported deals.
FCS players at an FBS-starter FV are priced at 40% of the FBS rate. CBB xNIL is minutes share × (BPM + 3) at the school's price.
entries.where: CFB board, team talent, team builder, fv to xNIL charts; CBB recruits

entries.short: Agencies ranked by tendency scores built from their clients, with the talent they represent.
body: Each client is one row in a ledger, named by the agency's own client page, an announcement or a report, with the source and its date. Family means a relative handles his deals and None means a source says he has no agent. A player no source names is left out.

Each score is a plus score, 100 + 25 × (s - the mean agency) / SD, so 100 is the average agency. s is the mean over the agency's clients pulled toward the mean of every represented client: (sum + k × mean) / (n + k), with k the spread inside agencies over the spread between them (8 or more until eight agencies have three or more clients).

Deal+ uses each college client's -zNIL over the sport's zNIL SD. Above 100 the agency gets its clients paid more than they are worth. Breakout+ uses FV minus the mean FV of board players with the same ARK stars and class. Above 100 its clients play above their high school grade.

A score is shown only where it held up on a split-half test: each agency's clients are split in two at random and the two half means are correlated across agencies, against 300 shuffles of the clients between agencies, and it has to clear p < .05 both weighted by clients and unweighted. Football: Deal r 0.53, p 0.033 (shipped); Situation r -0.40, p 0.867; Reach r 0.49, p 0.067; Breakout r 0.76, p 0.013 (shipped); Stability r -0.40, p 0.873. Basketball: Deal r -0.38, p 0.780; Situation r 0.23, p 0.240; Reach r -0.17, p 0.683; Breakout r 0.29, p 0.223. Situation is growth in FV over last season against players with the same FV and class, Reach is a power conference spot against players with the same FV and position, and Stability is staying at his school against players with the same FV and class.

Agency+ is the composite. Each part is z-scored across agencies and averaged: Deal as the shrunk edge, sum(v - mean) / (n + k), times the clients when it is above zero, so the same edge counts for more the more players it covers and a big roster is not charged per player for a low one, and sent, the drafted clients the agency had before the draft process (from 2027 on). Breakout+ is left out because it measures how good the clients turned out, not what the agency did for them. Deal only counts in a sport where it passed its test, so basketball has no Agency+ until its first tracked draft. A check on the 2022-26 search, which is not used: built from the clients on file and the 2022-24 sends, it ranks the 61 agencies by the first-round picks they sent in 2025-26 at Spearman 0.36 (p 0.002, 13 agencies with such a pick). Sends alone 0.22, Deal 0.13, Breakout -0.09, client count -0.15.

Drafted counts clients picked in the NFL or NBA draft who signed with the agency before the draft process began (declaring, or Dec 1 for football and Mar 15 for basketball). It does not count an agency a player signed with to go pro. It counts from the 2027 drafts on, every pick recorded on draft day. First-round picks from 2022-26 were searched too, but the sources on who had a player before he declared are too thin to judge an agency on, so they are kept on file and not counted. Pro% is drafted over drafted plus the college clients on file now.
Recruits count toward talent (FV, ARK stars) only. Low-confidence rows count toward talent only.
On file now: 225 football and 35 basketball players and recruits, 29 and 20 agencies.
entries.where: CFB and CBB agencies tabs, player and recruit cards

entries.short: A college player's on-field value for a season: snap share × position weight × quality.
body: Quality = Stat+ z + .5 badge z + .25 FV z. Team R² against 2026 SRS is .63, compared to .44 for summed FV value.
It is used for the cost of college injuries and for team value. NFL value stays on AV at FV.
entries.where: CFB team talent (Season AV), fv to war chart

entries.short: XPM (Cross Plus-Minus) is an NBA impact metric, .5 databallr DPM + .5 Basketball-Reference BPM, in points per 100 possessions over an average player, as played.
body: It is the headline XPM on every NBA board. O-XPM and D-XPM are the same blend for each side.
It includes BPM's team adjustment. Every player on a team moves by one amount on each side, so that minutes-weighted O-XPM × 5 = ORtg - league and D-XPM × 5 = league - DRtg.
Same-season team net R² is 0.999 (the box blend before the adjustment 0.963, BPM 0.988). Next season it is 0.647 (box blend 0.640, BPM 0.644).
The box blend before the adjustment feeds pXPM, the game models (which shrink it themselves) and the CBB board target. A player with no DPM row uses BPM alone (*).
The XPM and rookie boards default to qualified players, 1,000 MP per 82 team games. For qualified rookies 2010-23, XPM orders next-three-season VORX at .607 (VORX .604), and .330 for all rookies.
entries.where: NBA VORX/XPM leaders, rookies, team pages, ARKLIST

entries.short: Projected XPM for next season: XPM over three seasons by minutes, shrunk toward a role mean and aged. On the depth charts and backup watch it shrinks toward replacement.
body: Boards: (k × role mean + MP × XPM + w1 × MP-1 × XPM-1 + w2 × MP-2 × XPM-2) / (k + MP + w1 MP-1 + w2 MP-2) + the aging curve to next season.
k 200 MP, w1 0.35, w2 0.1, role mean = -3 + 1 ln(1 + MP82 / 100). Aging is the next-season change in XPM by age, fit on earlier seasons only.
Next-season XPM 2011-26, leaving one season out: RMSE 1.187, compared to 1.238 for a one-dial k 600 shrink and 1.58 raw (t = -7.28, 14/15 seasons).
Next-season team net rating, nine pairs, held out: R² 0.654, against rXPM 0.640, BPM 0.644, DPM 0.623 and the k 600 shrink 0.619.
Depth chart and backup watch: XPM over three seasons (minutes weighted 1, .5, .25) × M / (M + 500) + replacement (-1.4) × 500 / (M + 500).
entries.where: NBA VORX/XPM leaders (pXPM chip), rookies, depth chart, backup watch

entries.short: VORX (Value Over Replacement XPM) is NBA wins over replacement: .030 × (XPM + 1.4) × MP / 48.
body: Replacement is -1.4 XPM. Both constants are fit to team wins (480 team seasons 2011-26). It is the default sort on the XPM and rookie boards.

Team W% from minutes-weighted value, 2011-26: same-season R² is 0.938 on XPM, compared to 0.926 on the box blend before the team adjustment (t = 2.33, 10/13 seasons). Next season it is 0.679 compared to 0.681 (t = -0.25).
For rookies 2010-23, held out, VORX orders next-three-season VORX best (Spearman .398; pXPM .395, aXPM .379, XPM .330).
For next-three-season XPM, the rookie 3Y orders it best (.481; aXPM .413, XPM .417, VORX .351).
